passage_1.text:
In the late 1960s, while studying the northern-elephant-seal population along the coasts of Mexico and California, Burney Le Boeuf and his colleagues couldn't help but notice that the threat calls of males at some sites sounded different from those of males at other sites. That was the first time dialects were documented in a nonhuman mammal.

All the northern elephant seals that exist today are descendants of the small herd that survived on Isla Guadalupe after the near extinction of the species in the nineteenth century. As that tiny population grew, northern elephant seals started to recolonize former breeding locations. It was precisely on the more recently colonized islands where Le Boeuf found that the tempos of the male vocal displays showed stronger differences to the ones from Isla Guadalupe, the founder colony.

In order to test the reliability of these dialects over time, Le Boeuf and other researchers visited Año Nuevo Island in California - the island where males showed the slowest pulse rates in their calls every winter from 1968 to 1972. "What we found is that the pulse rate increased, but it still remained relatively slow compared to the other colonies we had measured in the past" Le Boeuf told me.

At the individual level, the pulse of the calls stayed the same: A male would maintain his vocal signature throughout his lifetime. But the average pulse rate was changing. Immigration could have been responsible for this increase, as in the early 1970s, 43 percent of the males on Año Nuevo had come from southern rookeries that had a faster pulse rate. This led Le Boeuf and his collaborator, Lewis Petrinovich, to deduce that the dialects were, perhaps, a result of isolation over time, after the breeding sites had been recolonized. For instance, the first settlers of Año Nuevo could have had, by chance, calls with low pulse rates. At other sites, where the scientists found faster pulse rates, the opposite would have happened - seals with faster rates would have happened to arrive first.

As the population continued to expand and the islands kept on receiving immigrants from the original population, the calls in all locations would have eventually regressed to the average pulse rate of the founder colony. In the decades that followed, scientists noticed that the geographical variations reported in 1969 were not obvious anymore. In the early 2010s, while studying northern elephant seals on Año Nuevo Island, researcher Caroline Casey noticed, too, that what Le Boeuf had heard decades ago was not what she heard now. By performing more sophisticated statistical analyses on both sets of data, Casey and Le Boeuf confirmed that dialects existed back then but had vanished. Yet there are other differences between the males from the late 1960s and their great-great-grandsons: Modern males exhibit more individual diversity, and their calls are more complex. While 50 years ago the drumming pattern was quite simple and the dialects denoted just a change in tempo, Casey explained, the calls recorded today have more complex structures, sometimes featuring doublets or triplets.

passage_2.text:
Vocabulary used in speech or writing organizes itself in seven parts of speech (eight, if you count interjections such as Oh! and Gosh! and Fuhgeddaboudit!). Communication composed of these parts of speech must be organized by rules of grammar upon which we agree. When these rules break down, confusion and misunderstanding result. Bad grammar produces bad sentences. My favorite example from Strunk and White is this one: "As a mother of five, with another one on the way, my ironing board is always up."

Nouns and verbs are the two indispensable parts of writing. Without one of each, no group of words can be a sentence, since a sentence is, by definition, a group of words containing a subject (noun) and a predicate (verb); these strings of words begin with a capital letter, end with a period, and combine to make a complete thought which starts in the writer's head and then leaps to the reader's.

Must you write complete sentences each time, every time? Perish the thought. If your work consists only of fragments and
floating clauses, the Grammar Police aren't going to come and take you away. Even William Strunk, that Mussolini of rhetoric,recognized the delicious pliability of language. "It is an old observation,” he writes, "that the best writers sometimes disregard the rules of rhetoric." Yet he goes on to add this thought, which I urge you to consider: "Unless he is certain of doing well, [the writer] will probably do best to follow the rules."

The telling clause here is Unless he is certain of doing well. If you don't have a rudimentary grasp of how the parts of speech translate into coherent sentences, how can you be certain that you are doing well? How will you know if you're doing ill, for that matter? The answer, of course, is that you can't, you won't. One who does grasp the rudiments of grammar finds a comforting simplicity at its heart, where there need be only nouns, the words that name, and verbs, the words that act.

Take any noun, put it with any verb, and you have a sentence. It never fails. Rocks explode. Jane transmits. Mountains float. These are all perfect sentences. Many such thoughts make little rational sense, but even the stranger ones (Plums deify!) have a kind of poetic weight that's nice. The simplicity of noun-verb construction is useful—at the very least it can provide a safety net for your writing. Strunk and White caution against too many simple sentences in a row, but simple sentences provide a path you can follow when you fear getting lost in the tangles of rhetoric all those restrictive and nonrestrictive clauses, those modifying phrases, those appositives and compound-complex sentences. If you start to freak out at the sight of such unmapped territory (unmapped by you, at least), just remind yourself that rocks explode, Jane transmits, mountains float, and plums deify. Grammar is the pole you grab to get your thoughts up on their feet and walking.

passage_4.text:
The word 'anarchy' comes from the Greek anarkhia, meaning contrary to authority or without a ruler, and was used in a derogatory sense until 1840, when it was adopted by Pierre-Joseph Proudhon to describe his political and social ideology. Proudhon argued that organization without government was both possible and desirable. In the evolution of political ideas, anarchism can be seen as an ultimate projection of both liberalism and socialism, and the differing strands of anarchist thought can be related to their emphasis on one or the other of these.

Historically, anarchism arose not only as an explanation of the gulf between the rich and the poor in any community, and of the reason why the poor have been obliged to fight for their share of a common inheritance, but as a radical answer to the question 'What went wrong?' that followed the ultimate outcome of the French Revolution. It had ended not only with a reign of terror and the emergence of a newly rich ruling caste, but with a new adored emperor, Napoleon Bonaparte, strutting through his conquered territories.

The anarchists and their precursors were unique on the political Left in affirming that workers and peasants, grasping the chance that arose to bring an end to centuries of exploitation and tyranny, were inevitably betrayed by the new class of politicians, whose first priority was to reestablish a centralized state power. After every revolutionary uprising, usually won at a heavy cost for ordinary populations, the new rulers had no hesitation in applying violence and terror, a secret police, and a professional army to maintain their control.

For anarchists the state itself is the enemy, and they have applied the same interpretation to the outcome of every revolution of the 19th and 20th centuries. This is not merely because every state keeps a watchful and sometimes punitive eye on its dissidents, but because every state protects the privileges of the powerful.

The mainstream of anarchist propaganda for more than a century has been anarchistcommunism, which argues that property in land, natural resources, and the means of production should be held in mutual control by local communities, federating for innumerable joint purposes with other communes. It differs from state socialism in opposing the concept of any central authority. Some anarchists prefer to distinguish between anarchist-communism and collectivist anarchism in order to stress the obviously desirable freedom of an individual or family to possess the resources needed for living, while not implying the right to own the resources needed by others.

There are, unsurprisingly, several traditions of individualist anarchism, one of them deriving from the 'conscious egoism' of the German writer Max Stirner (1806-56), and another from a remarkable series of 19th-century American figures who argued that in protecting our own autonomy and associating with others for common advantages, we are promoting the good of all. These thinkers differed from free-market liberals in their absolute mistrust of American capitalism, and in their emphasis on mutualism.

passage_7.text:
Few realise that the government of China, governing an empire of some 606060 million people during the Tang dynasty (618-907), implemented a complex financial system that recognized grain, coins and textiles as money. Coins did have certain advantages: they were durable, recognisable and provided a convenient medium of exchange, especially for smaller transactions. However, there were also disadvantages. A continuing shortage of copper meant that government mints could not produce enough coins for the entire empire, to the extent that for most of the dynasty's history, coins constituted only a tenth of the money supply. One of the main objections to calls for taxes to be paid in coin was that peasant producers who could weave cloth or grow grain the other two major currencies of the Tang would not be able to produce coins, and therefore would not be able to pay their taxes.

As coins had advantages and disadvantages, so too did textiles. If in circulation for a long period of time, they could show signs of wear and tear. Stained, faded and torn bolts of textiles had less value than a brand new bolt. Furthermore, a full bolt had a particular value. If consumers cut textiles into smaller pieces to buy or sell something worth less than a full bolt, that, too, greatly lessened the value of the textiles. Unlike coins, textiles could not be used for small transactions; as [an official] noted, textiles could not "be exchanged by the foot and the inch".

But textiles had some advantages over coins. For a start, textile production was widespread and there were fewer problems with the supply of textiles. For large transactions, textiles weighed less than their equivalent in coins since a string of coins. could weigh as much as 4 kg4 \mathrm{~kg}4 kg. Furthermore, the dimensions of a bolt of silk held remarkably steady from the third to the tenth century: 56 cm56 \mathrm{~cm}56 cm wide and 12 m12 \mathrm{~m}12 m long. The values of different textiles were also more stable than the fluctuating values of coins.

The government also required the use of textiles for large transactions. Coins, on the other hand, were better suited for smaller transactions, and possibly, given the costs of transporting coins, for a more local usage. Grain, because it rotted easily, was not used nearly as much as coins and textiles, but taxpayers were required to pay grain to the government as a share of their annual tax obligations, and official salaries were expressed in weights of grain.

In actuality, our own currency system today has some similarities even as it is changing in front of our eyes. We have cash coins for small transactions like paying for parking at a meter, and banknotes for other items; cheques and debit/credit cards for other, often larger, types of payments. At the same time, we are shifting to electronic banking and making payments online. Some young people never use cash and do not know how to write a cheque.

questions.question_text: All of the following can be inferred from Le Boeuf's study as described in the passage EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: male northern elephant seals might not have exhibited dialects had they not become nearly extinct in the nineteenth century.

options.label: B
options.text: the average call pulse rate of male northern elephant seals at Año Nuevo Island increased from the early 1970s till the disappearance of dialects.

options.label: C
options.text: changes in population and migration had no effect on the call pulse rate of individual male northern elephant seals.

options.label: D
options.text: the influx of new northern elephant seals into Año Nuevo Island would have soon made the call pulse rate of its male seals exceed that of those at Isla Guadalupe..

questions.explanation_text:
Need to find what the passage doesn't support or what contradicts it.

From passage: "As the population continued to expand and the islands kept on receiving immigrants from the original population, the calls in all locations would have eventually regressed to the average pulse rate of the founder colony."

The key insight -> the passage explains that immigrant seals would make all locations move toward the founder colony's average rate, not exceed it.

Elimination Strategy:

Look for direct support in passage -> three options will have clear backing, one won't.

🟢 Option 1 -> supported -> passage shows near extinction led to isolation and recolonization, which created dialects

🟢 Option 2 -> supported -> passage states pulse rate increased at Año Nuevo, and dialects later disappeared

🟢 Option 3 -> supported -> passage clearly states "A male would maintain his vocal signature throughout his lifetime"

🔴 Option 4 -> contradicts passage -> passage says immigration would make rates "regress to the average pulse rate of the founder colony" (Isla Guadalupe), meaning they'd move toward that rate, not exceed it

The passage explains that as immigrants from the original population (Isla Guadalupe) joined other colonies, the call rates would converge toward the founder colony's average. Option 4 suggests the opposite - that rates would exceed the founder colony's rate. This directly contradicts the passage's explanation of how migration affects call patterns.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following conditions, if true, could have ensured that male northern elephant seal dialects did not disappear?

options.label: A
options.text: Besides Isla Guadalupe, there was one more surviving colony with the same average male call tempo from which no migration took place.

options.label: B
options.text: The call tempo of individual immigrant male seals changed to match the average tempo of resident male seals in the host colony.

options.label: C
options.text: Besides Isla Guadalupe, there was one more founder colony with the same average male call tempo from which male seals migrated to various other colonies.

options.label: D
options.text: The call tempo of individual male seals in host colonies changed to match the average call tempo of immigrant male seals.

questions.explanation_text:
To solve this,we need to understand why dialects disappeared and what could have prevented it.

From passage: "As the population continued to expand and the islands kept on receiving immigrants from the original population, the calls in all locations would have eventually regressed to the average pulse rate of the founder colony."

The dialects vanished because -> immigrants brought their original call patterns -> this mixed with local patterns -> averaged out to founder colony's pattern -> local distinctiveness lost.

For dialects to survive -> we need to stop this averaging process -> immigrants must NOT change the local pattern.

🔴 Option 1 -> irrelevant -> Even if one colony stops sending migrants, other colonies (including Guadalupe) still send them. The averaging problem continues.

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> If immigrants adopt local patterns instead of bringing their own, local dialects stay pure and distinctive. No averaging happens.

🔴 Option 3 -> worsens problem -> More colonies sending migrants with founder patterns makes averaging happen faster, not slower.

🔴 Option 4 -> opposite of solution -> This describes exactly what happened and caused dialect loss. Residents changing to match immigrants is the problem, not the solution.

The trick is recognizing that behavioral adaptation by immigrants (not migration patterns) would preserve local dialects.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following best sums up the overall history of transformation of male northern elephant seal calls?

options.label: A
options.text: The calls have transformed from exhibiting simple composition, less individual variety, and great regional variety to complex composition, great individual variety, and less regional variety.

options.label: B
options.text: Owing to migrations in the aftermath of near species extinction, the calls have transformed from exhibiting complex composition, less individual variety, and great regional variety to simple composition, less individual variety, and great regional variety.

options.label: C
options.text: The calls have transformed from exhibiting simple composition, less individual variety, and great regional variety to complex composition, less individual variety, and great regional variety.

options.label: D
options.text: Owing to migrations in the aftermath of near species extinction, the average call pulse rates in the recolonised breeding locations exhibited a gradual increase until they matched the tempo at the founding colony.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage gives us a clear before-and-after picture.

From passage: "Modern males exhibit more individual diversity, and their calls are more complex. While 50 years ago the drumming pattern was quite simple and the dialects denoted just a change in tempo, Casey explained, the calls recorded today have more complex structures"

From passage: "In the decades that followed, scientists noticed that the geographical variations reported in 1969 were not obvious anymore"

The transformation path: Simple + Regional variety → Complex + Individual variety

Now let's check each option against this timeline:

🟢 Option 1 is correct → captures the complete transformation accurately

  • Gets all three changes right: simple→complex, less individual→more individual, great regional→less regional

🔴 Option 2 → direction-error → says calls got simpler when they got more complex

  • Completely backwards on complexity trend

🟠 Option 3 → partial-truth → right about complexity but wrong about individual variety

  • Says individual variety stayed low when passage clearly states it increased

🔴 Option 4 → scope-error → too narrow, misses the big picture

  • Only talks about pulse rates matching founder colony, ignores complexity and individual diversity changes entirely

The key insight: Option 1 captures all three dimensions of change (composition, individual variety, regional variety) while others miss at least one major transformation.

questions.question_text: From the passage it can be inferred that the call pulse rate of male northern elephant seals in the southern rookeries was faster because:

options.label: A
options.text: a large number of male northern elephant seals migrated from the southern rookeries to Año Nuevo Island in the early 1970s

options.label: B
options.text: a large number of male northern elephant seals from Año Nuevo Island might have migrated to the southern rookeries to recolonise them.

options.label: C
options.text: the male northern elephant seals of Isla Guadalupe with faster call pulse rates might have been the original settlers of the southern rookeries.

options.label: D
options.text: the calls of male northern elephant seals in the southern rookeries have more sophisticated structures, containing doublets and triplets.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find why southern rookeries had faster pulse rates. The key is understanding how different colonies developed their own dialects after recolonization.

From passage: "This led Le Boeuf and his collaborator, Lewis Petrinovich, to deduce that the dialects were, perhaps, a result of isolation over time, after the breeding sites had been recolonized. For instance, the first settlers of Año Nuevo could have had, by chance, calls with low pulse rates. At other sites, where the scientists found faster pulse rates, the opposite would have happened—seals with faster rates would have happened to arrive first."

The logic works like this: All seals came from Isla Guadalupe originally -> They spread out to recolonize different areas -> By random chance, seals with certain pulse rates settled in certain areas -> Año Nuevo got slow-pulse settlers -> Southern rookeries got fast-pulse settlers -> Over time, these became regional dialects.

Students often get confused between options 1 and 3 because both mention southern rookeries and migration. But option 1 talks about later migration in the 1970s, while the question asks about the original reason for faster pulse rates.

🟠 Option 1 -> timeline-error -> talks about 1970s migration to Año Nuevo, not why southern rookeries originally had faster rates

🟠 Option 2 -> direction-error -> suggests migration from Año Nuevo to southern rookeries, but passage shows all colonies came from Isla Guadalupe

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> explains original settlement pattern: faster-pulse seals from Isla Guadalupe happened to settle southern rookeries first

🟠 Option 4 -> time-period-error -> describes modern call complexity, not historical pulse rates that created the dialects

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements, if false, could be seen as supporting the arguments in the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: An understanding of grammar helps a writer decide if she/he is writing well or not.

options.label: B
options.text: Regarding grammar, women writers tend to be more attentive to method and accuracy.

options.label: C
options.text: It has been observed that writers sometimes disregard the rules of rhetoric.

options.label: D
options.text: Perish the thought that complete sentences necessarily need nouns and verbs!

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "Nouns and verbs are the two indispensable parts of writing. Without one of each, no group of words can be a sentence"

From passage: "Take any noun, put it with any verb, and you have a sentence. It never fails."

The passage strongly argues that nouns and verbs are essential for sentences -> So if someone said "complete sentences don't need nouns and verbs" and that turned out to be false, it would actually support what the author is saying.

Think of it this way: If your friend disagrees with you, but then their disagreement proves to be wrong, that actually supports your original point!

🟠 Option 1 -> actually-supports-passage -> The passage directly says understanding grammar helps you know if you're writing well. If this were false, it would contradict the passage, not support it.

🔴 Option 2 -> irrelevant -> The passage never mentions women writers specifically. Whether this is true or false doesn't relate to the author's arguments about grammar and sentence structure.

🟠 Option 3 -> stated-as-true -> The passage explicitly says "the best writers sometimes disregard the rules of rhetoric." Since this matches what's in the passage, making it false would contradict the author.

🟢 Option 4 -> opposite-of-passage -> This statement goes directly against the passage's main argument that nouns and verbs are "indispensable." If this statement were false (meaning sentences DO need nouns and verbs), it would perfectly support the author's central point about sentence construction.

questions.question_text: "Take any noun, put it with any verb, and you have a sentence. It never fails. Rocks explode. Jane transmits. Mountains float." None of the following statements can be seen as similar EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: A collection of people with the same sports equipment is a sports team.

options.label: B
options.text: Take any vegetable, put some spices in it, and you have a dish.

options.label: C
options.text: A group of nouns arranged in a row becomes a sentence.

options.label: D
options.text: Take an apple tree, plant it in a field, and you have an orchard

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which option follows the same pattern as the original quote about making sentences.

From passage: "Take any noun, put it with any verb, and you have a sentence. It never fails. Rocks explode. Jane transmits. Mountains float."

The passage shows a simple formula: Take Element A + Element B = Complete Thing. The author says this formula always works and gives examples to prove it.

Let's check what makes this formula special:

  • Uses "Take any X, put it with Y" structure
  • Claims it creates something complete
  • Says the method "never fails"
  • Gives examples that work

Now we need to find which option uses the same type of formula.

🔴 Option 1 -> wrong-structure -> "A collection of people with the same sports equipment is a sports team" - This is just a definition, not a formula. No "take X, put it with Y" pattern.

🟢 Option 2 -> correct-match -> "Take any vegetable, put some spices in it, and you have a dish" - Perfect! Same formula structure: Take X + put Y with it = complete thing. This formula makes sense and would work.

🔴 Option 3 -> wrong-content -> "A group of nouns arranged in a row becomes a sentence" - Wrong about grammar (sentences need verbs too!) and doesn't use the formula structure.

🔴 Option 4 -> logic-fails -> "Take an apple tree, plant it in a field, and you have an orchard" - Uses similar structure BUT one tree doesn't make an orchard. The original emphasized the formula "never fails" but this one fails the logic test.

Only Option 2 copies both the formula structure and the logical success of the original statement.

questions.question_text: Inferring from the passage, the author could be most supportive of which one of the following practices?

options.label: A
options.text: The availability of language software that will standardise the rules of grammar as an aid to writers

options.label: B
options.text: A campaign demanding that a writer's creative license should allow the breaking of grammatical rules.

options.label: C
options.text: A Creative Writing course that focuses on how to avoid the use of rhetoric.

options.label: D
options.text: The critique of standardised rules of punctuation and capitalisation.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what practice the author would support based on their views about grammar and writing rules.

Let us trace the author's key beliefs:

The author believes grammar rules are helpful tools, not restrictions. They provide structure when writers need it.

From passage: "Grammar is the pole you grab to get your thoughts up on their feet and walking."

The author also says experienced writers can break rules, but only if they know what they're doing:

From passage: "Unless he is certain of doing well, [the writer] will probably do best to follow the rules."

So the author supports: Grammar knowledge → Safety net for writers → Better writing

🟢 Option 1 is correct → Language software standardizing grammar rules as aid to writers - This matches perfectly! The author sees grammar as helpful structure ("safety net", "pole to grab"). Software that helps writers follow grammar rules would support the author's view that grammar helps writing.

🔴 Option 2 → irrelevant → Campaign for breaking grammar rules - Author says break rules only if you're "certain of doing well." A general campaign to break rules would create the "confusion" the author warns against.

🔴 Option 3 → context-shift → Avoiding rhetoric in Creative Writing - Author calls Strunk "Mussolini of rhetoric" but doesn't say avoid rhetoric completely. Author talks about navigating "tangles of rhetoric," not eliminating it.

🔴 Option 4 → opposite-view → Critiquing punctuation/capitalization rules - Author supports rules and structure. Critiquing standardized rules goes against the author's belief that rules prevent "confusion and misunderstanding."

The author wants grammar to help writers, not restrict them. Option 1 provides helpful tools while Options 2 and 4 attack the rules system, and Option 3 misunderstands the author's view on rhetoric.

questions.question_text: All of the following statements can be inferred from the passage EXCEPT that.

options.label: A
options.text: “Grammar Police” is a metaphor for critics who focus on linguistic rules.

options.label: B
options.text: sentences do not always have to be complete.

options.label: C
options.text: the subject–predicate relation is the same as the noun–verb relation

options.label: D
options.text: the primary purpose of grammar is to ensure that sentences remain simple.

questions.explanation_text:
Three options will be supported by the text, but one won't be.

From passage: "Must you write complete sentences each time, every time? Perish the thought. If your work consists only of fragments and floating clauses, the Grammar Police aren't going to come and take you away."

The author talks about grammar's role -> organizing communication -> preventing confusion. Simple sentences are presented as a safety net, not the main goal.

🟢 Option 1 -> clearly supported -> "Grammar Police" is obviously a playful metaphor for people who criticize bad grammar

🟢 Option 2 -> directly stated -> author says "Perish the thought" about always writing complete sentences, mentions fragments are okay

🟢 Option 3 -> explicitly defined -> passage says "subject (noun) and a predicate (verb)" - directly equates them

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> confuses a tool with the purpose. Passage says simple sentences are a "safety net" when you get lost in complex grammar, but the primary purpose of grammar is to organize communication and prevent confusion, not to keep things simple. Author even mentions complex structures like "restrictive clauses" and "compound-complex sentences" as normal parts of grammar.

The key trap here: students might think simple = good, so grammar must want simplicity. But the passage shows grammar handles both simple and complex structures - simplicity is just one option, not the main goal.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following quotes best captures the main concern of the passage?

options.label: A
options.text: "Nouns and verbs are the two indispensable parts of writing. Without one of each, no group of words can be a sentence."

options.label: B
options.text: "Strunk and White caution against too many simple sentences in a row, but simple sentences provide a path you can follow when you fear getting lost in the tangles of rhetoric."

options.label: C
options.text: "Bad grammar produces bad sentences."

options.label: D
options.text: "The telling clause here is Unless he is certain of doing well."

questions.explanation_text:
First,we need to identify what the passage is really about -> The author talks about grammar rules, how they organize communication, and what happens when they break down.

From passage: "When these rules break down, confusion and misunderstanding result. Bad grammar produces bad sentences."

The author's main worry -> Poor grammar creates communication problems. Everything else (nouns/verbs, simple sentences, breaking rules) supports this central concern.

Now let's eliminate the wrong options by checking what each quote focuses on:

🟠 Option 1 -> scope-error -> focuses only on sentence construction basics, not the broader concern about grammar problems

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> mentions simple sentences as a tool but misses the main worry about bad grammar causing communication issues

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> directly states the core problem the author is concerned about throughout the passage

🟠 Option 4 -> context-shift -> about being careful before breaking rules, but doesn't capture the main concern about grammar's importance

The key insight: Option 3 gives us the cause and effect that drives the whole passage -> bad grammar causes bad sentences, which causes communication problems. This is what the author keeps coming back to and wants us to understand.

questions.question_text: According to the passage, what is the one idea that is common to all forms of anarchism?

options.label: A
options.text: They all focus on the primacy of the power of the individual.

options.label: B
options.text: They all derive from the work of Pierre-Joseph Proudhon.

options.label: C
options.text: There is no idea common to all forms of anarchism; that is why it is anarchic.

options.label: D
options.text: They are all opposed to the centralisation of power in the state.

questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "The word 'anarchy' comes from the Greek anarkhia, meaning contrary to authority or without a ruler"

From passage: "For anarchists the state itself is the enemy"

From passage: "It differs from state socialism in opposing the concept of any central authority"

The passage shows different types -> anarchist-communism, collectivist anarchism, individualist anarchism -> but they all share one core belief about opposing centralized state power.

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> only applies to individualist anarchism, not to anarchist-communism which focuses on communities working together, not individual power

🔴 Option 2 -> factually wrong -> passage clearly states individualist anarchism comes from Max Stirner and American thinkers, not from Proudhon's work

🔴 Option 3 -> contradicts passage -> passage actually shows there is a common idea - opposition to centralized authority runs through all types mentioned

🟢 Option 4 is correct -> captures the core theme that appears in every section -> the very definition of anarchy means "without a ruler" -> all types oppose centralized state power, whether they're communist-style or individualist-style anarchists

questions.question_text: Of the following sets of concepts, identify the set that is conceptually closest to the concerns of the passage.

options.label: A
options.text: Revolution, State, Protection, Liberals.

options.label: B
options.text: Anarchism, Betrayal, Power, State.

options.label: C
options.text: Revolution, State, Strike, Egoism.

options.label: D
options.text: Anarchism, State, Individual, Freedom.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find which set of four concepts best captures what the passage is really about. From passage: "The anarchists and their precursors were unique on the political Left in affirming that workers and peasants, grasping the chance that arose to bring an end to centuries of exploitation and tyranny, were inevitably betrayed by the new class of politicians"

From passage: "There are, unsurprisingly, several traditions of individualist anarchism... who argued that in protecting our own autonomy and associating with others for common advantages, we are promoting the good of all"

The passage covers: anarchism's definition -> why it arose (failed revolutions) -> anarchist view of state as enemy -> different types of anarchism (especially individual vs collective focus).

🔴 Option 1 -> scope-error -> completely misses the main topic! The passage is fundamentally about anarchism, but this option doesn't even include the word. It's like writing about dogs and then listing "animals, food, exercise, veterinarians" - you missed the main subject.

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> includes anarchism and state (good!), mentions betrayal (which appears in passage), but "betrayal" is more of a supporting detail rather than a core concept. The passage uses betrayal to explain why anarchism developed, but it's not a central ongoing concern.

🔴 Option 3 -> scope-error -> same problem as option 1 - misses "anarchism" entirely! Plus "strike" barely appears in the passage, while "egoism" is just mentioned briefly about one thinker (Max Stirner).

🟢 Option 4 -> captures core themes -> includes anarchism (main topic), state (what anarchists oppose), individual (major focus - individualist anarchism gets significant coverage), and freedom (the ultimate goal - "obviously desirable freedom of an individual").

The key insight: this passage balances discussing anarchism as both a collective movement and an individual philosophy. Option 4 captures both dimensions perfectly.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following best expresses the similarity between American individualist anarchists and free-market liberals as well as the difference between the former and the latter?

options.label: A
options.text: Both prioritise individual autonomy; but the former also emphasise mutual dependence, while the latter do not do so.

options.label: B
options.text: Both reject the regulatory power of the state; but the former favour a people's state, while the latter favour state intervention in markets.

options.label: C
options.text: Both are sophisticated arguments for capitalism; but the former argue for a morally upright capitalism, while the latter argue that the market is the only morality.

options.label: D
options.text: Both are founded on the moral principles of altruism; but the latter conceive of the market as a force too mystical for the former to comprehend.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what American individualist anarchists and free-market liberals share, and how they differ. Let us trace through the passage to find this comparison.

The key is in the last paragraph where it directly compares these two groups.we need to look for both similarities and differences mentioned there.

From passage: "These thinkers differed from free-market liberals in their absolute mistrust of American capitalism, and in their emphasis on mutualism."

The passage shows American individualist anarchists "argued that in protecting our own autonomy and associating with others for common advantages, we are promoting the good of all."

So the thought process: Both groups care about individual autonomy -> but American individualist anarchists also stress mutualism (working together) -> while free-market liberals don't emphasize this mutual cooperation.

🔴 Option 2 -> context-shift -> says American individualist anarchists "favour a people's state" but passage says they're anarchists who oppose centralized authority completely

🔴 Option 3 -> contradicts passage -> claims both are "arguments for capitalism" but passage clearly states American individualist anarchists had "absolute mistrust of American capitalism"

🔴 Option 4 -> irrelevant -> talks about "mystical" markets and altruism principles not mentioned anywhere in passage

🟢 Option 1 is correct -> captures both the shared focus on individual autonomy and the key difference that American individualist anarchists emphasize mutualism while free-market liberals do not

The passage directly supports this: both protect "our own autonomy" but American individualist anarchists add "associating with others for common advantages" (mutualism) which free-market liberals don't emphasize.

questions.question_text: The author makes all of the following arguments in the passage, EXCEPT:

options.label: A
options.text: The failure of the French Revolution was because of its betrayal by the new class of politicians who emerged from it.

options.label: B
options.text: Individualist anarchism is actually constituted of many streams, all of which focus on the autonomy of the individual.

options.label: C
options.text: The popular perception of anarchism as espousing lawlessness and violence comes from a mainstream mistrust of collectivism.

options.label: D
options.text: For anarchists, the state is the enemy because all states apply violence and terror to maintain their control.

questions.explanation_text:
Let's check each option against the passage carefully.

Step-by-step process:

First, scan the passage for evidence of each claim -> then identify which one has no support in the text.

For EXCEPT questions: 3 options will be clearly supported by the passage, 1 option will be missing or contradicted.

From passage: "The word 'anarchy' comes from the Greek anarkhia, meaning contrary to authority or without a ruler, and was used in a derogatory sense until 1840"

The passage mentions the derogatory sense but doesn't explain why people have this negative view -> this is key for elimination.

🟢 Option 1 -> clearly supported -> passage directly states French Revolution ended with "new class of politicians" who betrayed the cause

🟢 Option 2 -> clearly supported -> passage mentions "several traditions of individualist anarchism" focusing on "autonomy"

🔴 Option 3 -> not argued -> passage mentions anarchism was viewed negatively but never explains this comes from "mainstream mistrust of collectivism"

🟢 Option 4 -> clearly supported -> passage states "every state" uses "violence and terror" to maintain control

Key elimination insight: The passage talks about anarchism's negative reputation but doesn't give the reason for this reputation. Option 3 provides a specific explanation (mistrust of collectivism) that simply isn't in the text.

Students often get confused between "anarchism was viewed negatively" (which is mentioned) and "the reason for this negative view" (which isn't explained). The passage describes the historical fact but not the psychological/social cause.

questions.question_text: The author believes that the new ruling class of politicians betrayed the principles of the French Revolution, but does not specify in what way. In the context of the passage, which statement below is the likeliest explanation of that betrayal?

options.label: A
options.text: The new ruling class struck a deal with the old ruling class to share power between them.

options.label: B
options.text: The new ruling class rode to power on the strength of the workers' revolutionary anger, but then turned to oppress that very class.

options.label: C
options.text: The new ruling class was constituted mainly of anarchists who were against the destructive impact of the Revolution on the market.

options.label: D
options.text: The anarchists did not want a new ruling class, but were not politically strong enough to stop them.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage explains how the French Revolution ended badly, but we need to figure out exactly how the new politicians betrayed the people who fought for change.

From passage: "workers and peasants, grasping the chance that arose to bring an end to centuries of exploitation and tyranny, were inevitably betrayed by the new class of politicians, whose first priority was to reestablish a centralized state power"

The thought process: Workers and peasants fought the revolution -> New politicians came to power because of this fight -> These same politicians then used their power against the workers and peasants

From passage: "After every revolutionary uprising, usually won at a heavy cost for ordinary populations, the new rulers had no hesitation in applying violence and terror, a secret police, and a professional army to maintain their control"

This shows the betrayal clearly: The people who helped them get power became their victims.

🔴 Option 1 -> irrelevant -> talks about deals with old ruling class, but passage never mentions this happening

🟢 Option 2 -> correct -> perfectly matches the passage's logic: workers helped politicians gain power, then politicians oppressed those same workers

🔴 Option 3 -> context-shift -> completely wrong because anarchists were against centralized power, not part of the new ruling class

🔴 Option 4 -> scope-error -> talks about anarchist political strength, but question asks about how betrayal happened, not why anarchists couldn't stop it

The key insight: The betrayal was the classic "use people to get power, then turn against them" pattern that the passage describes happening after revolutions.

questions.question_text: According to the passage, the modern currency system shares all the following features with that of the Tang, EXCEPT that:

options.label: A
options.text: it uses different materials as currency

options.label: B
options.text: it is undergoing transformation

options.label: C
options.text: its currencies fluctuate in value over time

options.label: D
options.text: it uses different currencies for different situations

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what modern currency does NOT share with Tang currency. From passage: "In actuality, our own currency system today has some similarities even as it is changing in front of our eyes."

The passage shows both systems use different materials -> Tang used grain, coins, textiles while modern uses cash, banknotes, cards. Both systems use different currencies for different situations -> Tang used coins for small transactions and textiles for large ones, modern uses cash for parking meters and cards for larger payments.

Nowwe need to spot what's unique to modern currency:

From passage: "even as it is changing in front of our eyes. At the same time, we are shifting to electronic banking and making payments online."

This talks about ongoing transformation happening right now in modern currency. The Tang passage describes a stable system over centuries but doesn't mention it changing or transforming during that period.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> Both systems use different materials (Tang: grain/coins/textiles, Modern: cash/cards/banknotes)

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> Tang had "fluctuating values of coins" mentioned, modern currencies also fluctuate

🟠 Option 4 -> partial-truth -> Both use different currencies for different situations (Tang: coins for small, textiles for large; Modern: cash for meters, cards for bigger purchases)

🟢 Option 2 is correct -> Only modern currency is described as "changing" and "shifting to electronic banking" - Tang system is presented as established, not transforming

questions.question_text: When discussing textiles as currency in the Tang period, the author uses the words “steady” and “stable” to indicate all of the following EXCEPT

options.label: A
options.text: reliable quality

options.label: B
options.text: reliable supply

options.label: C
options.text: reliable transportation

options.label: D
options.text: reliable measurements

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what "steady" and "stable" don't refer to when talking about textiles as money in Tang China.

First, locate where the author uses "steady" and "stable" -> these key words appear in paragraph 3 where the author lists textile advantages.

From passage: "Furthermore, the dimensions of a bolt of silk held remarkably steady from the third to the tenth century: 56 cm wide and 12 m long. The values of different textiles were also more stable than the fluctuating values of coins."

Now we can see exactly what "steady" and "stable" describe -> measurements stayed the same for centuries, and values didn't change as much as coin values did.

The passage also mentions supply advantages -> "textile production was widespread and there were fewer problems with the supply of textiles" but doesn't use "steady" or "stable" for this.

For transportation, the passage says textiles were lighter than coins -> but again, no "steady" or "stable" language here.

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> the stable values could suggest reliable quality, but this stretches the meaning

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> supply is mentioned as reliable, but not called "steady" or "stable"

🟢 Option 3 -> correct answer -> transportation advantages are mentioned (lighter weight) but never described as "steady" or "stable"

🟠 Option 4 -> directly stated -> "dimensions held remarkably steady" explicitly refers to measurements

The key insight: while textiles had transportation benefits, the author never uses "steady" or "stable" to describe reliable transportation. Those words specifically describe measurements and values only.

questions.question_text: During the Tang period, which one of the following would not be an economically sound decision for a small purchase in the local market that is worth one-eighth of a bolt of cloth?

options.label: A
options.text: Cutting one-eighth of the fabric from a new bolt to pay the amount.

options.label: B
options.text: Using coins issued by the government to make the payment.

options.label: C
options.text: Making the payment with the appropriate weight of grain.

options.label: D
options.text: Paying with a faded bolt of cloth that has approximately the same value.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what would NOT be economically sound for a small purchase worth one-eighth of a bolt of cloth.

Let us trace through the passage to understand the Tang currency system -> coins good for small transactions -> textiles better for large transactions -> grain less commonly used but acceptable.

From passage: "If consumers cut textiles into smaller pieces to buy or sell something worth less than a full bolt, that, too, greatly lessened the value of the textiles."

The key insight -> cutting textiles destroys their value -> full bolts maintain value but pieces lose significant worth -> this makes cutting economically wasteful.

Also important -> "textiles could not be exchanged by the foot and the inch" -> confirms textiles weren't meant for small transactions.

🔴 Option 1 -> economically unsound -> cutting one-eighth from a new bolt would "greatly lessen the value" according to the passage -> you'd lose money by destroying a valuable full bolt

🟢 Option 2 -> economically sound -> coins were specifically good for "smaller transactions" -> perfect for this purchase size

🟢 Option 3 -> economically sound -> grain was accepted as payment even if less common -> no indication it's economically wasteful

🟢 Option 4 -> economically sound -> faded bolt still maintains full bolt value -> better than cutting a new bolt -> doesn't destroy value structure

The passage clearly states cutting textiles into pieces "greatly lessened the value" -> Option 1 is the only economically unsound choice because you'd waste money by destroying a valuable full bolt for a small purchase.

questions.question_text:
In the context of the passage, which one of the following can be inferred with regard to the use of currency during the Tang
era?

options.label: A
options.text: Copper coins were more valuable and durable than textiles.

options.label: B
options.text: Currency that deteriorated easily was not used for official work.

options.label: C
options.text: Grains were the most used currency because of government requirements.

options.label: D
options.text: Currency usage was similar to that of modern times.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what can be inferred about Tang dynasty currency use from the passage. Let us trace through the key information step by step.

The passage describes three types of money: coins, textiles, and grain. Each had specific uses -> coins for small transactions, textiles for large transactions, grain for taxes and official salaries. The final paragraph makes a direct comparison to modern times.

From passage: "In actuality, our own currency system today has some similarities even as it is changing in front of our eyes. We have cash coins for small transactions like paying for parking at a meter, and banknotes for other items; cheques and debit/credit cards for other, often larger, types of payments."

The key insight -> passage explicitly compares Tang currency system to modern times, showing how different currencies served different transaction sizes and purposes, just like today.

🔴 Option 1 -> degree-error -> Says coins were "more valuable" than textiles, but passage never compares their values directly. Actually shows coins had supply problems (only 1/10 of money supply due to copper shortage).

🔴 Option 2 -> contradicts passage -> Claims deteriorating currency wasn't used officially, but grain "rotted easily" yet was required for taxes and "official salaries were expressed in weights of grain."

🔴 Option 3 -> contradicts passage -> Says grain was "most used," but passage clearly states grain "was not used nearly as much as coins and textiles" due to rotting problems.

🟢 Option 4 -> directly supported -> The entire last paragraph makes this exact comparison, explaining how Tang dynasty had different currencies for different transaction types, just like we use cash for small purchases, cards for larger ones, and electronic payments today.

The confusion might be between options 2 and 4, but option 2 is clearly wrong because grain was officially used despite deteriorating. Option 4 has explicit textual support in the final paragraph's comparison.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. For feminists, the question of how we read is inextricably linked with the question of what we read.
  2. Elaine Showalter's critique of the literary curriculum is exemplary of this work.
  3. Androcentric literature structures the reading experience differently depending on the gender of the reader.
  4. The documentation of this realization was one of the earliest tasks undertaken by feminist critics.
  5. More specifically, the feminist inquiry into the activity of reading begins with the realization that the literary canon is androcentric, and that this has a profoundly damaging effect on women readers.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "More specifically, the feminist inquiry into the activity of reading begins with the realization that the literary canon is androcentric" and "The documentation of this realization was one of the earliest tasks undertaken by feminist critics."

Thought Process:

Look for connecting words and references -> "More specifically" in sentence 5 connects to sentence 1 -> "this realization" in sentence 4 points back to sentence 5 -> sentence 2 gives an example with "this work" -> sentence 3 talks about similar topics but doesn't connect to the flow

How to eliminate:

  • Find the chain of connection between sentences
  • Look for reference words like "this," "more specifically," "this work"
  • One sentence will feel disconnected from the main flow

The logical flow is: 1 → 5 → 4 → 2

Sentence 1 introduces feminist reading concerns → Sentence 5 uses "More specifically" to elaborate → Sentence 4's "this realization" refers back to sentence 5's point about androcentric canon → Sentence 2 gives Showalter as an example of "this work"

🟢 Sentence 3 is the odd one out → disconnected flow → While it talks about androcentric literature affecting readers differently by gender, it doesn't connect to the specific chain of ideas about feminist criticism documenting the problems with literary canon. It's a related but separate point that breaks the logical sequence.

The other four sentences form a complete argument: feminist reading concerns → specific realization about androcentric canon → early feminist critics documented this → Showalter as example.

Answer: 3

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

For years, movies and television series like Crime Scene Investigation (CSI) paint an unrealistic picture of the "science of voices." In the 1994 movie Clear and Present Danger an expert listens to a brief recorded utterance and declares that the speaker is "Cuban, aged 35 to 45, educated in the eastern United States." The recording is then fed to a supercomputer that matches the voice to that of a suspect, concluding that the probability of correct identification is 90%. This sequence sums up a good number of misimpressions about forensic phonetics, which have led to errors in real-life justice. Indeed, that movie scene exemplifies the so-called "CSI effect" the phenomenon in which judges hold unrealistic expectations of the capabilities of forensic science.

options.label: A
options.text: Movies and televisions have led to the belief that the use of forensic phonetics in legal investigations is robust and fool proof.

options.label: B
options.text: Voice recognition as used in many movies to identify criminals has been used to identify criminals in real life also.

options.label: C
options.text: Voice recognition has started to feature prominently in crime-scene intelligence investigations because of movies and television series.

options.label: D
options.text: Although voice recognition is often presented as evidence in legal cases, its scientific basis can be shaky.

questions.explanation_text:
The passage criticizes how movies and TV shows create unrealistic expectations about voice forensics. The key is connecting media influence -> unrealistic beliefs -> problems in real justice.

From passage: "movies and television series like Crime Scene Investigation (CSI) paint an unrealistic picture of the 'science of voices'... which have led to errors in real-life justice"

Thought Process:

Movies show voice analysis as super accurate -> judges believe this is real -> they expect too much from actual voice evidence -> this causes justice system problems

The passage structure: Media portrayal -> unrealistic expectations -> real-world consequences

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures both the media influence AND the unrealistic belief that forensic phonetics is "robust and fool proof" - exactly what the passage argues against

🔴 Option 2 -> tone-error -> sounds positive about voice recognition working in real life, but the passage warns it creates unrealistic expectations and causes errors in justice

🟠 Option 3 -> partial-truth -> mentions movies/TV influence but misses the key point that these expectations are unrealistic - just says voice recognition "features prominently" without the criticism

🟠 Option 4 -> scope-error -> talks about shaky scientific basis (true) but completely ignores the movies/TV influence which is the main focus of the passage

The confusion here is between options 1 and 4 - both mention problems with voice forensics. But option 4 misses the media influence angle that drives the entire passage.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Tensions and sometimes conflict remain an issue in and between the 11 states in South East Asia (Brunei Darussalam, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos, Malaysia, Myanmar, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand, Timor-Leste and Vietnam).
  2. China's rise as a regional military power and its claims in the South China Sea have become an increasingly pressing security concern for many South East Asian states.
  3. Since the 1990s, the security environment of South East Asia has seen both continuity and profound changes.
  4. These concerns cause states from outside the region to take an active interest in South Asian security.
questions.explanation_text:
Step 1: Find the topic sentence

Sentence 3 mentions "Since the 1990s" and talks about both continuity and profound changes -> This is clearly the opening because it sets up the whole discussion.

Step 2: What shows "continuity"?

Sentence 1 says tensions "remain an issue" -> The word "remain" shows something continuing from before.

Step 3: What shows "profound changes"?

Sentence 2 talks about "China's rise" -> This is clearly a new development, representing change.

Step 4: What's the consequence?

Sentence 4 starts with "These concerns" -> This must refer to the concerns about China mentioned in sentence 2.

From passage: "Since the 1990s, the security environment of South East Asia has seen both continuity and profound changes."

Logical flow: Topic sentence (3) -> Example of continuity (1) -> Example of change (2) -> Consequence of the change (4)

The sequence is 3-1-2-4:

• Sentence 3 introduces the framework (continuity + changes)

• Sentence 1 shows continuity (ongoing tensions)

• Sentence 2 shows change (China's rise)

• Sentence 4 shows the result (outside interest due to these concerns)

The pronoun "These concerns" in sentence 4 clearly connects back to China's security concerns mentioned in sentence 2, making this the correct ending.

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Relying on narrative structure alone, indigenous significances of nineteenth century San folktales are hard to determine.
  2. Using their supernatural potency, benign shamans transcend the levels of the San cosmos in order to deal with social conflict and to protect material resources and enjoy a measure of respect that sets them apart from ordinary people.
  3. Selected tales reveal that they deal with a form of spiritual conflict that has social implications and concern conflict between people and living or dead malevolent shamans.
  4. Meaning can be elicited, and the tales contextualized, by probing beneath the narrative of verbatim, original-language records and exploring the connotations of highly significant words and phrases.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: Sentence 1 sets up a problem - "indigenous significances of nineteenth century San folktales are hard to determine" when relying only on narrative structure.

The thought process: Start with the broadest statement -> then look for solution -> then specific findings -> then details

Step-by-step logic:

  • Sentence 1 = Problem statement (most general)
  • Sentence 4 = Solution to that problem
  • Sentence 3 = What the solution reveals
  • Sentence 2 = Details about shamans mentioned in 3

Connection Analysis:

1→4: Sentence 1 says significance is "hard to determine" → Sentence 4 explains how meaning "can be elicited" by probing deeper

4→3: Sentence 4 talks about probing beneath narratives → Sentence 3 shows what "selected tales reveal" when you do this probing

3→2: Sentence 3 mentions "malevolent shamans" → Sentence 2 describes shamans and their powers in detail

From passage: "Selected tales reveal that they deal with a form of spiritual conflict...concerning conflict between people and living or dead malevolent shamans" flows into describing what shamans actually do.

The sequence 1432 creates a clear logical progression: Problem → Solution → Discovery → Elaboration.

Any other sequence would break this natural flow from general problem to specific details about shamans.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

For nearly a century most psychologists have embraced one view of intelligence. Individuals are born with more or less intelligence potential (I.Q.); this potential is heavily influenced by heredity and difficult to alter; experts in measurement can determine a person's intelligence early in life, currently from paper-and-pencil measures, perhaps eventually from examining the brain in action or even scrutinizing his/her genome. Recently, criticism of this conventional wisdom has mounted. Biologists ask if speaking of a single entity called "intelligence" is coherent and question the validity of measures used to estimate heritability of a trait in humans, who, unlike plants or animals, are not conceived and bred under controlled conditions.

options.label: A
options.text: Biologists have criticised that conventional wisdom that individuals are born with more or less intelligence potential.

options.label: B
options.text: Biologists have started questioning psychologists' view of 'intelligence' as a measurable immutable characteristic of an individual.

options.label: C
options.text: Biologists have questioned the long-standing view that 'intelligence' is a single entity and the attempts to estimate it's heritability.

options.label: D
options.text: Biologists have questioned the view that 'intelligence' is a single entity and the ways in which what is inherited.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what biologists are specifically questioning about the traditional psychology view of intelligence.

From passage: "Biologists ask if speaking of a single entity called 'intelligence' is coherent and question the validity of measures used to estimate heritability of a trait in humans"

The passage shows: Traditional psychology view -> biologists criticize -> two main questions arise

Step 1: Traditional view = intelligence is inherited, measurable, single thing

Step 2: Biologists challenge this -> ask two specific questions

Step 3: Question 1 = Is intelligence even one single entity?

Step 4: Question 2 = Can we properly measure how it's inherited in humans?

Now we need to find which option captures both criticisms accurately:

🟠 Option 1 -> partial-truth -> only mentions being "born with potential" but misses the two key criticisms about single entity and measuring heritability

🟠 Option 2 -> degree-error -> says "immutable" but passage says "difficult to alter" (not impossible). Also misses the specific criticisms biologists made

🟢 Option 3 -> correct -> captures both main criticisms: questioning intelligence as "single entity" AND questioning "attempts to estimate heritability"

🔴 Option 4 -> context-shift -> mentions "single entity" correctly but second part "ways in which what is inherited" is confusing and inaccurate - biologists questioned measuring heritability, not inheritance ways

The key confusion students have: Options 3 and 4 both mention "single entity" so they seem similar. But Option 4's second part doesn't match what biologists actually questioned. They questioned measuring heritability, not inheritance itself.

questions.question_text:
The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

As Soviet power declined, the world became to some extent multipolar, and Europe strove to define an independent identity. What a journey Europe has undertaken to reach this point. It had in every century changed its internal structure and invented new ways of thinking about the nature of international order. Now at the culmination of an era, Europe, in order to participate in it, felt obliged to set aside the political mechanisms through which it had conducted its affairs for three and a half centuries. Impelled also by the desire to cushion the emergent unification of Germany, the new European Union established a common currency in 2002 and a formal political structure in 2004. It proclaimed a Europe united, whole, and free, adjusting its differences by peaceful mechanisms.

options.label: A
options.text: Europe has chosen to lower political and economic heterogeneity, in order to adapt itself to an emerging multi-polar world.

options.label: B
options.text: The establishment of a formal political structure in Europe was hastened by the unification of Germany and the emergence of a multipolar world.

options.label: C
options.text: Europe has consistently changed its internal structure to successfully adapt to the changing world order.

options.label: D
options.text: Europe has consistently changed in keeping with the changing world order and that has culminated in a united Europe.

questions.explanation_text:
We need to find what Europe did and why they did it. From passage: "As Soviet power declined, the world became to some extent multipolar, and Europe strove to define an independent identity... the new European Union established a common currency in 2002 and a formal political structure in 2004."

The passage shows a clear cause and effect -> Soviet decline made world multipolar -> Europe responded by creating both economic unity (common currency) and political unity (formal structure).

Now we need to find which option captures both what Europe did and why they did it:

🟢 Option 1 -> correct -> captures both economic changes (common currency) and political changes (formal structure) as "lowering heterogeneity." Also correctly identifies the cause as "emerging multi-polar world"

🟠 Option 2 -> partial-truth -> only mentions political structure, completely ignores the economic part (common currency). A student might pick this because it mentions Germany and multipolar world, but it's incomplete.

🟠 Option 3 -> too-generic -> says "changing world order" instead of the specific "multipolar world." Also doesn't capture the recent specific changes (currency + political structure). This sounds right but lacks the precision of Option 1.

🟠 Option 4 -> degree-error -> "united Europe" overstates what happened. The passage talks about EU, not all of Europe. Also uses vague "changing world order" instead of specific "multipolar world."

The key insight: Option 1 is specific and complete, while others either miss parts or use vague language where the passage is specific.

questions.question_text:
Five jumbled up sentences (labelled 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5), related to a topic, are given below. Four of them can be put together to form a coherent paragraph. Identify the odd sentence and key in the number of that sentence as your answer.

  1. Talk was the most common way for enslaved men and women to subvert the rules of their bondage, to gain more agency than they were supposed to have.
  2. Even in conditions of extreme violence and unfreedom, their words remained ubiquitous, ephemeral, irrepressible, and potentially transgressive.
  3. Slaves came from societies in which oaths, orations, and invocations carried great potency, both between people and as a connection to the all-powerful spirit world.
  4. Freedom of speech and the power to silence may have been preeminent markers of white liberty in Colonies, but at the same time, slavery depended on dialogue: slaves could never be completely muted.
  5. Slave-owners obsessed over slave talk, though they could never control it, yet feared its power to bind and inspire—for, as everyone knew, oaths, whispers, and secret conversations bred conspiracy and revolt.
questions.explanation_text:
Sentences 1, 2, 4, 5: All focus on slave speech during slavery - how they used talk, how owners feared it, how it couldn't be stopped

  • Sentence 3: Talks about where slaves came from before slavery and their original societies

From passage: "Slaves came from societies in which oaths, orations, and invocations carried great potency, both between people and as a connection to the all-powerful spirit world."

The key insight -> Sentence 3 shifts to cultural background (spirit world, original societies) while others stay focused on speech during slavery.

How to eliminate easily:

🟢 Sentence 3 is the odd one -> context-shift -> brings in "spirit world" and "societies they came from" which isn't discussed anywhere else. All other sentences stay focused on slave talk during slavery, not before it.

The other four sentences (1, 2, 4, 5) connect smoothly -> They discuss how slave talk was used for resistance -> how it couldn't be controlled -> why owners feared it -> how it remained powerful despite attempts to silence it.

Answer: 3

questions.question_text:
The sentences given below, when properly sequenced, would yield a coherent paragraph. Decide on the proper sequencing of the order of the sentences and key in the sequence of the numbers as your answer.

  1. Man has used poisons for assassination purposes ever since the dawn of civilization, against individual enemies but also occasionally against armies.
  2. These dangers were soon recognized, and resulted in two international declarations- in 1874 in Brussels and in 1899 in The Hague-that prohibited the use of poisoned weapons.
  3. The foundation of microbiology by Louis Pasteur and Robert Koch offered new prospects for those interested in biological weapons because it allowed agents to be chosen and designed on a rational basis.
  4. Though treaties were all made in good faith, they contained no means of control, and so failed to prevent interested parties from developing and using biological weapons.
questions.explanation_text:
From passage: "These dangers were soon recognized" (sentence 2) and "Though treaties were all made in good faith" (sentence 4)

Step-by-step thinking process:

Find the starting sentence -> Look for connecting words -> Follow the timeline -> Check references between sentences

Elimination Strategy:

🟢 Sentence 1 must come first -> Most general topic introduction + mentions "dawn of civilization" (earliest time period)

🟠 Sentence 3 comes next -> Talks about new scientific developments that created fresh dangers/prospects for biological weapons

🟠 Sentence 2 follows sentence 3 -> "These dangers were soon recognized" directly refers to the new prospects mentioned in sentence 3

🟠 Sentence 4 comes last -> "Though treaties" refers back to the "declarations" mentioned in sentence 2

Key connector words that seal the deal:

  • "These dangers" in sentence 2 -> needs something dangerous mentioned before it (sentence 3's "new prospects")
  • "Though treaties" in sentence 4 -> needs treaties mentioned before it (sentence 2's "declarations")

Final sequence: 1-3-2-4 = 1324

The sentences flow chronologically from ancient times -> scientific advancement -> international response -> failure of agreements.
